items.claim: Where a target enforces a weak password policy, the absence of login throttling can be proven by registering a throwaway account with a very weak password and then issuing unlimited login attempts against it.
items.body:
Where a target enforces a weak password policy, the absence of login throttling can be proven by registering a throwaway account with a very weak password and then issuing unlimited login attempts against it.

HackTricks reference: account takeovers methods (https://kathan19.gitbook.io/howtohunt/account-takeover-methodology/account_takeovers_methods.md)
items.disproof: The login endpoint applies account lockout, login throttling or a challenge after a small number of attempts, so the extra attempts never reach password checking.

items.claim: The password reset response body is worth inspecting for a reset link, token or OTP, because a token handed back in the response is directly replayable instead of only being mailed to the account owner.
items.body:

items.disproof: The reset response carries no link, token or OTP, and the reset step stays gated on out-of-band delivery to the registered mailbox.

items.claim: A JSON response body that states whether 2FA authentication succeeded is the field to manipulate, because the client-visible success value is what the 2FA check may be read from.
items.body:
A JSON response body that states whether 2FA authentication succeeded is the field to manipulate, because the client-visible success value is what the 2FA check may be read from.

HackTricks reference: 2fa bypasses (https://kathan19.gitbook.io/howtohunt/authentication-bypass/2fa_bypasses.md)
items.disproof: Editing the success field in the 2FA response body leaves the session unauthenticated because the server records the verified state independently of the returned JSON.

sources.quote:
Response Manipulation

Some 2FA implementations return a JSON response indicating whether authentication was successful.

A protection space is defined by the canonical root URI (the scheme and authority components of the effective request URI; see Section 5.5 of [RFC7230]) of the server being accessed, in combination with the realm value if present.
In return, the response time will be different for the same error, allowing the attacker to differentiate between a wrong username and a wrong password.

items.claim: Some applications decide 2FA authentication success from the HTTP status code of the verification request, so a verification that returns a non-success status can still leave the client treating the second factor as passed.
items.body:
Some applications decide 2FA authentication success from the HTTP status code of the verification request, so a verification that returns a non-success status can still leave the client treating the second factor as passed.

HackTricks reference: 2fa bypasses (https://kathan19.gitbook.io/howtohunt/authentication-bypass/2fa_bypasses.md)
items.disproof: Changing or suppressing the status code of the verification response does not change client state, which follows a server-set authenticated session flag instead.
